questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at its centre. The length of the chord (in cm) is:
questions.solution:
Join the centre $O$ to the two ends $A$ and $B$ of the chord. Both $OA$ and $OB$ are radii, so

$OA = OB = 10$ cm and $\angle AOB = 90°$

That makes $\triangle OAB$ a right-angled triangle with the chord as its hypotenuse. By Pythagoras:

$AB = \sqrt{10^{2} + 10^{2}} = \sqrt{200} = \mathbf{10\sqrt{2}}$ cm

No circle theorem is needed — the two radii and the chord simply **are** a right triangle, and an isosceles one at that.

A quick check on size: the chord must be shorter than the diameter (20 cm) and longer than the radius. $10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.1$ sits nicely between.

questions.q: If $PQ$ and $PR$ are tangents to a circle with centre $O$ and radius 4 cm such that $\angle QPR = 90°$, then the length $OP$ is:
questions.solution:
**A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact**, so

$\angle OQP = \angle ORP = 90°$

In quadrilateral $OQPR$ the four angles add to $360°$, and three of them are $90°$ ($\angle Q$, $\angle R$ and $\angle QPR$). So $\angle QOR = 90°$ too — all four angles are right angles, and since $OQ = OR = 4$ (both radii), $OQPR$ is a **square** of side 4.

$OP$ is its diagonal:

$OP = 4\sqrt{2}$ cm

Or straight from $\triangle OQP$, right-angled at $Q$ with $\angle OPQ = 45°$ (the $90°$ at $P$ is split equally by $OP$):

$\sin 45° = \dfrac{4}{OP} \Rightarrow OP = 4\sqrt{2}$ cm ✓

The fact that unlocks nearly every tangent question is the right angle at the point of contact. Draw the radii to the contact points first, before anything else.

questions.q: The length of the tangent drawn from a point 13 cm away from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm is:
questions.solution:
Let $P$ be the external point, $O$ the centre and $T$ the point of contact. The radius $OT$ meets the tangent at right angles, so $\triangle OTP$ is right-angled **at $T$** — with $OP = 13$ as the hypotenuse.

$PT = \sqrt{OP^{2} - OT^{2}} = \sqrt{13^{2} - 5^{2}} = \sqrt{169 - 25} = \sqrt{144} = \mathbf{12}$ cm

Option (D), $\sqrt{194}$, is what you get by **adding** the squares — treating $OP$ as a leg instead of the hypotenuse. The distance from the external point to the centre is always the longest side, because it faces the right angle.

$5, 12, 13$ again: the same triple that turns up throughout this syllabus.

questions.q: The number of tangents that can be drawn to a circle from a point lying **inside** the circle is:
questions.solution:
A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point and never enters it. A line through a point **inside** the circle must cut straight across and come out the other side — so it meets the circle **twice**, which makes it a secant, not a tangent.

So the answer is **$0$**: no tangent can be drawn from an interior point.

The full picture is worth holding as a set of three:

- point **inside** the circle → **0** tangents
- point **on** the circle → **1** tangent (at that very point)
- point **outside** the circle → **2** tangents, and they are equal in length

Each case follows from the same idea: how many lines through the point can touch without crossing.

questions.q: $PA$ and $PB$ are two tangents drawn from an external point $P$ to a circle with centre $O$. If $\angle APB = 60°$, then $\angle AOB$ is:
questions.solution:
Draw the radii to the two points of contact. Since a tangent meets the radius at right angles,

$\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90°$

In quadrilateral $OAPB$ the angles add to $360°$:

$\angle AOB + 90° + 60° + 90° = 360°$

$\angle AOB = \mathbf{120°}$

The general rule falls straight out of that: $\angle AOB$ and $\angle APB$ always add to $180°$ — they are **supplementary**. Squeeze the tangents together and the angle at the centre opens up, and vice versa.

A useful special case to remember: if the tangents are perpendicular ($\angle APB = 90°$), then $\angle AOB = 90°$ as well, and the figure is a square — which is exactly the earlier question about $OP = 4\sqrt{2}$.

questions.q: The angle between a tangent to a circle and the radius drawn at the point of contact is:
questions.solution:
The answer is **$90°$** — this is the single most-used fact in the whole chapter.

Why it must be so: of all the lines from the centre to the tangent line, the radius to the point of contact is the **shortest**, because every other point of the tangent lies outside the circle and is therefore further than one radius away. And the shortest line from a point to a line is always the perpendicular.

Everything else in this chapter is built on it — equal tangent lengths, the supplementary-angle result, the perpendicular bisector property. When a tangent appears, draw that radius.

questions.topic: Chord tangent to an inner circle
questions.q: Two concentric circles have radii 5 cm and 3 cm. Find the length, in centimetres, of a chord of the larger circle which touches the smaller circle.
questions.solution:
Let $O$ be the common centre, $AB$ the chord of the larger circle, and $P$ the point where it touches the smaller one.

**Use the tangent property.** $AB$ is a tangent to the small circle at $P$, so $OP \perp AB$ and $OP = 3$ cm.

**Use the chord property.** A perpendicular from the centre to a chord **bisects** it, so $P$ is the mid-point of $AB$.

Now in the right triangle $OPA$, with $OA = 5$ (radius of the larger circle):

$AP = \sqrt{5^{2} - 3^{2}} = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$ cm

and the whole chord is twice that:

$AB = 2 \times 4 = \mathbf{8}$ cm

Two facts meet at the point $P$ — it is both the point of contact (so the radius is perpendicular) and the mid-point of the chord (so the halves are equal). Forgetting to double $AP$ at the end is the usual slip.

questions.q: A circle is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ touching $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ at $P$, $Q$ and $R$ respectively. If $AP = 4$ cm, $BP = 6$ cm and $CR = 5$ cm, find the perimeter of the triangle in centimetres.
questions.solution:
**The key fact:** the two tangents drawn to a circle from the same external point are **equal in length**.

Apply it at each vertex:

From $A$: $AP = AR = 4$ cm

From $B$: $BP = BQ = 6$ cm

From $C$: $CR = CQ = 5$ cm

Now build the three sides:

$AB = AP + PB = 4 + 6 = 10$ cm

$BC = BQ + QC = 6 + 5 = 11$ cm

$CA = CR + RA = 5 + 4 = 9$ cm

**Perimeter** $= 10 + 11 + 9 = \mathbf{30}$ cm

Notice the shortcut hiding in it: the perimeter is $2(4 + 6 + 5) = 30$, because every tangent length gets counted exactly twice as you walk round the triangle.

The picture is a piece of string wrapped tight around a circle: each straight run appears once on the way out from a corner and once on the way back to the next.

questions.topic: Tangents at the ends of a chord
questions.q: Prove that the tangents drawn at the end points of a chord of a circle make equal angles with the chord.
questions.solution:
**Given.** A circle with centre $O$ and a chord $AB$. Tangents at $A$ and $B$ meet at $P$.

**To prove.** $\angle PAB = \angle PBA$

**Proof.** The two tangents are drawn from the same external point $P$, and tangents from an external point are equal in length:

$PA = PB$

So $\triangle PAB$ is **isosceles**, with $PA$ and $PB$ as its equal sides.

In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. The angle opposite $PA$ is $\angle PBA$, and the angle opposite $PB$ is $\angle PAB$. Therefore

$\angle PAB = \angle PBA$ ∎

Those are exactly the angles the two tangents make with the chord $AB$.

The proof is three lines long because all the work is in the first one. "Tangents from an external point are equal" turns a circle problem into an isosceles-triangle problem, and the rest is a fact from Class 9.

(If the tangents are parallel — when $AB$ is a diameter — there is no point $P$, but then both angles are $90°$ and the result still holds.)

questions.q: Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
questions.solution:
**Given.** A parallelogram $ABCD$ circumscribing a circle, touching $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ at $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ respectively.

**To prove.** $ABCD$ is a rhombus, i.e. all four sides are equal.

**Proof.** Tangents from an external point are equal, so at each vertex:

$AP = AS$ … (1)

$BP = BQ$ … (2)

$CR = CQ$ … (3)

$DR = DS$ … (4)

Add all four:

$AP + BP + CR + DR = AS + BQ + CQ + DS$

Group them into whole sides:

$(AP + PB) + (CR + RD) = (AS + SD) + (BQ + QC)$

$AB + CD = AD + BC$ … (5)

Now use the parallelogram. Opposite sides are equal:

$AB = CD$ and $AD = BC$

Substituting into (5):

$2AB = 2AD \Rightarrow AB = AD$

So two adjacent sides are equal, and with $AB = CD$ and $AD = BC$ that makes **all four sides equal**. A parallelogram with all sides equal is a rhombus. ∎

Step (5) is worth remembering on its own: **in any quadrilateral circumscribing a circle, the two pairs of opposite sides have equal sums.** The parallelogram condition is then just what collapses that into all-sides-equal.

questions.q: From an external point $P$, two tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn to a circle with centre $O$. Prove that $OP$ is the perpendicular bisector of the chord $AB$.
questions.solution:
**Given.** Tangents $PA$ and $PB$ from an external point $P$ to a circle with centre $O$. Let $OP$ meet $AB$ at $M$.

**To prove.** $AM = MB$ and $OP \perp AB$.

**Proof.** Compare $\triangle PAM$ and $\triangle PBM$:

$PA = PB$ (tangents from an external point) … (1)

$\angle APM = \angle BPM$ ($OP$ bisects the angle between the tangents, since $\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP$ by RHS: $OA = OB$ as radii, $OP$ common, and right angles at $A$ and $B$) … (2)

$PM = PM$ (common) … (3)

By **SAS**, $\triangle PAM \cong \triangle PBM$.

Therefore, by CPCT:

$AM = MB$ … so $M$ is the mid-point of $AB$

and

$\angle AMP = \angle BMP$

But these two angles sit on the straight line $AB$, so they add to $180°$. Being equal, each must be $90°$:

$OP \perp AB$

Hence $OP$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. ∎

The pattern is worth naming: prove two triangles congruent, then read off **both** conclusions from CPCT. The equal halves give the bisector; the equal angles on a straight line give the perpendicular.

questions.q: Prove that the opposite sides of a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle subtend supplementary angles at the centre of the circle.
questions.solution:
**Given.** Quadrilateral $ABCD$ circumscribing a circle with centre $O$, touching $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ at $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$.

**To prove.** $\angle AOB + \angle COD = 180°$ (and likewise $\angle BOC + \angle AOD = 180°$).

**Proof.** Join $O$ to $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and to $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$.

From vertex $A$ the tangents are $AP$ and $AS$, and

$\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OAS$ (RHS: $OP = OS$ radii, $OA$ common, right angles at $P$ and $S$)

so $\angle AOP = \angle AOS$. Call each of these $\angle 1$; similarly write the eight small angles at $O$ as $\angle 1, \angle 1, \angle 2, \angle 2, \angle 3, \angle 3, \angle 4, \angle 4$ going round.

All eight fill a complete turn:

$2(\angle 1 + \angle 2 + \angle 3 + \angle 4) = 360°$

$\angle 1 + \angle 2 + \angle 3 + \angle 4 = 180°$ … (∗)

Now, $\angle AOB$ is made of the two angles either side of the contact point $P$, and $\angle COD$ of the two either side of $R$. Between them they account for one of each pair:

$\angle AOB + \angle COD = (\angle 1 + \angle 2) + (\angle 3 + \angle 4) = 180°$ by (∗) ∎

The same counting gives $\angle BOC + \angle AOD = 180°$.

The engine of the proof is that each vertex's two tangents are mirror images in the line joining the vertex to the centre — so the eight little angles at $O$ come in four equal pairs, and a full turn splits neatly in half.

questions.q: Prove that the angle between the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle is supplementary to the angle subtended by the line segment joining the points of contact at the centre.
questions.solution:
**Given.** A circle with centre $O$; tangents from an external point $P$ touch it at $A$ and $B$.

**To prove.** $\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180°$

**Proof.** A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so

$\angle OAP = 90°$ and $\angle OBP = 90°$

Now look at quadrilateral $OAPB$. The angles of any quadrilateral add to $360°$:

$\angle AOB + \angle OAP + \angle APB + \angle PBO = 360°$

$\angle AOB + 90° + \angle APB + 90° = 360°$

$\angle AOB + \angle APB = 180°$ ∎

So the two angles are supplementary.

**Sanity check with a picture.** Stand far from the circle and the two tangents are nearly parallel — $\angle APB$ is tiny, and the chord $AB$ (almost a diameter) subtends nearly $180°$ at the centre. Walk closer and $\angle APB$ opens up while $\angle AOB$ closes down, the two always totalling a straight angle.

The whole proof rests on the two right angles. Draw the radii to the points of contact and the quadrilateral does the arithmetic for you.

questions.topic: Tangent length and a right triangle
questions.q: A tangent $PQ$ at a point $P$ of a circle of radius 5 cm meets a line through the centre $O$ at a point $Q$ such that $OQ = 13$ cm. Find the length of $PQ$.
questions.solution:
**Draw the radius to the point of contact.** $OP$ is a radius and $PQ$ is a tangent at $P$, so

$OP \perp PQ$, i.e. $\angle OPQ = 90°$

That makes $\triangle OPQ$ right-angled at $P$, with $OQ$ as the hypotenuse.

**Apply Pythagoras:**

$OQ^{2} = OP^{2} + PQ^{2}$

$13^{2} = 5^{2} + PQ^{2}$

$169 = 25 + PQ^{2}$

$PQ^{2} = 144 \Rightarrow PQ = \mathbf{12}$ cm

**Check the sides make sense:** $5, 12, 13$ is a right triangle ✓ and the hypotenuse $OQ = 13$ is the longest, as it must be.

The one decision in this question is **where** the right angle is. It is at $P$, the point of contact — not at $Q$ and not at $O$. Get that right and Pythagoras finishes it in one line.

questions.q: Prove that in any quadrilateral $ABCD$ circumscribing a circle, $AB + CD = AD + BC$.
questions.solution:
**Given.** Quadrilateral $ABCD$ circumscribing a circle, touching $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ at $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ respectively.

**To prove.** $AB + CD = AD + BC$

**Proof.** Tangents drawn from an external point are equal, so at each of the four vertices:

$AP = AS$ … (1)

$BP = BQ$ … (2)

$CR = CQ$ … (3)

$DR = DS$ … (4)

Add (1), (2), (3) and (4):

$AP + BP + CR + DR = AS + BQ + CQ + DS$

Regroup the left side into two whole sides, and the right side into the other two:

$(AP + PB) + (CR + RD) = (AS + SD) + (BQ + QC)$

$AB + CD = AD + BC$ ∎

**A way to see it without algebra.** Walk around the quadrilateral, and mark each tangent segment with the vertex it comes from: $a, a, b, b, c, c, d, d$. One pair of opposite sides collects $a + b$ and $c + d$; the other pair collects $a + d$ and $b + c$. Both totals come to $a + b + c + d$ — every tangent length counted exactly once.

This is the result that made the rhombus proof work, and it is worth knowing on its own.
